fetched_contents.text: Cytomegalovirus infection in non-immunocompromised critically ill patients: A management perspective Abstract Critically ill patients are a vulnerable group at high risk of developing secondary infections. High disease severity, prolonged intensive care unit (ICU) stay, sepsis, and multiple drugs with immunosuppressive activity make these patients prone to immuneparesis and increase the risk of various opportunistic infections, including cytomegalovirus (CMV). CMV seroconversion has been reported in up to 33% of ICU patients, but its impact on patient outcomes remains a matter of debate. Even though there are guidelines regarding the management of CMV infection in immunosuppressive patients with human immunodeficiency virus/ acquired immuno deficiency syndrome, the need for treatment and therapeutic approaches in immunocompetent critically ill patients is still ambiguous. Even the diagnosis of CMV infection may be challenging in such patients due to non-specific symptoms and multiorgan involvement. Hence, a better understanding of the symptomatology, diagnostics, and treatment options may aid intensive care physicians in ensuring accurate diagnoses and instituting therapeutic interventions. Keywords: Cytomegalovirus, Critically ill, Immunocompetent, Intensive care unit, Virus ---------------------------------------- Core Tip: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) reactivation in critically ill immunocompetent patients may lead to increased intensive care unit (ICU) and hospital mortality, prolonged mechanical ventilation, longer ICU stay and increased risk of secondary bacterial and fungal infections. Nevertheless, whether it is the cause of clinical deterioration or is just a marker of disease severity remains debatable. Hence, the need for any therapeutic intervention is a management conundrum. The data extrapolated from studies on immunocompromised patients may not apply to these otherwise immunocompetent patients. This warrants future large-scale prospective studies on CMV reactivation in immunocompetent critically ill patients. INTRODUCTION Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is a known opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients and a predictor of poor outcomes. It has been extensively studied in post-transplant patients, human immunodeficiency virus/acquired immunodeficiency syndrome and neonates. Critically ill patients represent a sick cohort with risk factors like multiple comorbidities, sepsis, high disease severity, prolonged intensive care unit (ICU) stay and medications with immunosuppressive effects. All these can cause immunoparesis, even in patients with no previous history of immunosuppression, making them prone to opportunistic infections. A systematic review of 13 studies with 1258 critically ill immunocompetent patients showed the rate of active CMV infection to be 17% (95%CI, 11% to 24%). This review defined active CMV infection as a single positive result for polymerase chain reaction (PCR), CMV antigen (pp65) or viral culture[1]. The test used for defining active CMV infection has an impact on the prevalence. In a prospective study of 120 non-immunocompromised patients admitted in ICU who were CMV seropositive, the reactivation rate was 33% when real-time PCR was used, indicating a high disease burden in modern ICUs[2]. CMV reactivation was found to be associated with increased hospital stay or 30 d ICU mortality. Patients with severe sepsis and high disease severity had a CMV infection rate of 32% which was significantly higher to an average of 17% (P < 0.0001). Patients with active CMV infection also had a higher mortality rate with an odds ratio (OR) of 1.93 (95%CI, 1.29 to 2.88; P < 0.001)[1]. A meta-analysis which included 18 observational studies with almost 2400 immunocompetent critically ill patients, CMV reactivation rate was 31% (95%CI 24%-39%), with the OR for all-cause mortality rate with and without CMV infection being 2.16 (95%CI 1.70-2.74). However, the same study showed no effect on mortality when the analysis was limited to detecting CMV in blood[3]. This raises the dilemma of CMV positivity being a marker of severe illness carrying poor prognosis rather than a direct causative factor of increased mortality. We conducted a systematic search from the databases of PubMed, Reference Citation Analysis (https://www.referencecitationanalysis.com/), EMBASE and Google Scholar from all the past studies till July 2023. The search terms included major MESH terms "Cytomegalovirus", "CMV", and "Non-immunocompromised" or "Immunocompetent". The results were filtered for the studies published in the English language and for adult patients (> 18 years). Studies with non-critically ill patients were also excluded. We manually screened the results and included the relevant literature. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY CMV is the commonest herpes viridae to infect humans. It is a double-stranded DNA virus with 165 genes which encode viral proteins that interact with host proteins. After an acute or primary infection, the virus enters a latent phase, which the presence of immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies can detect. The seroprevalence of CMV IgG antibodies in women of childbearing age in India is almost 80%–90%. In contrast, it is less than 50% in developed countries, showing a greater baseline prevalence in developing countries[4,5]. During the latent phase, CMV remains latent in dendritic cells and monocytes. The cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocyte suppress viral gene replication. Secondary symptomatic disease occurs due to the reactivation of latent infection during a state of decreased immunity or secondary infection with a new strain. fetched_contents.text: Cytomegalovirus reactivation in ICU patients Abstract Introduction Approximately 20 years have passed since we reported our results of histologically proven cytomegalovirus (CMV) pneumonia in non-immunocompromised ICU patients. Even if there are more recent reports suggesting that CMV may worsen the outcomes for ICU patients, there is no definite answer to this question: is CMV a potential pathogen for ICU patients or is it simply a bystander? Methods We will describe the pathophysiology of active CMV infection and the most recent insights concerning the epidemiological aspects of these reactivations. Major findings Cytomegalovirus can be pathogenic by a direct organ insult (such as for the lung), by decreasing host defences against other microorganisms and/or by enhancing the body’s inflammatory response (as in acute respiratory distress syndrome). The incidence of active CMV infection is dependent on the diagnostic method used. Using the most sophisticated available biological tools, the incidence can reach 15–20 % of ICU patients (20–40 % in ICU patients with positive CMV serology). In adequately powered cohorts of patients, active CMV infection appears to be associated with worse outcomes for mechanically ventilated ICU patients. Discussion There is no absolute direct proof of a negative impact of active CMV infection on the health outcomes of mechanically ventilated patients. Prospective randomized trials are lacking. Future trials should examine the potential benefits for health outcomes of using antiviral treatments. Such treatments could be prophylactic, pre-emptive or used only when there is an end-organ disease. Conclusion Cytomegalovirus infection may affect health outcomes for ICU patients. Additional prospective trials are necessary to confirm this hypothesis. Keywords: Cytomegalovirus, ICU, Mechanical ventilation, Mortality, Incidence, Reactivation Introduction Primary infection due to cytomegalovirus (CMV) is generally asymptomatic or characterized by the presence of non-specific signs and symptoms. Previous infection is confirmed by the presence of CMV-specific IgG responses. Approximately 60–80 % of immunocompetent adults are human CMV seropositive [1, 2]. Following primary infection, CMV remains quiescent in monocytes and macrophages in multiple organs, a state defined as latency. As with other herpesviridae, this harbouring of latent CMV makes this affected population at risk for reactivation, especially during critical illness. Primary infection or reinfection with a different strain of CMV during the ICU stay is theoretically possible (blood products) but is unlikely due to leucoreduction processes. While the potential for CMV reactivation in ICU patients is now acknowledged, much controversy remains over its pathogenicity. Indeed, CMV could be pathogenic or simply an associated sign reflecting the severity of underlying disease. Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain how CMV reactivation could cause injury. The first is a direct cytopathologic effect from the reactivated virus injuring organs that harboured the virus such as during CMV pneumonia [3–5]. The second mechanism is an immunopathological effect, in which damage to tissues is caused by the excessive immune response to the virus such as that hypothesised in ARDS patients [6]. The third mechanism is related to an alteration of patients’ immune defences, rendering them more susceptible to fungal and bacterial infections [7–10]. However, CMV reactivation could only be an indicator of immune compromise and illness severity not necessitating diagnostic procedures and treatment. Why we did this study As with many things in medicine, our story began with an unexpected observation, which occurred during the controversy between intensive care practitioners who maintained the use of a protected specimen brush (PSB) for the diagnosis of bacteriological ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) and those who preferred the use of tracheal aspirates (TA) (as we did). This was the reason why we designed a study evaluating the diagnostic performance of several microbiological sampling techniques such as PSB, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), TA and protected telescopic catheter for the diagnosis of VAP [11]. The gold standard was lung histology and lung culture following pneumonectomy. Our work has had two major consequences. First, our surgical colleagues became convinced that performing an open-lung biopsy (OLB) was feasible at the bedside, in the ICU, in mechanically ventilated patients. It was why we started to perform OLBs at the bedside [5]. The second consequence was that our pathologist colleagues reported that in some instances they did not identify any sign of bacterial pneumonia but found typical signs of CMV pneumonia that were confirmed using specific immunological markers. After a dubitative period, we decided to extend the use of OLBs, especially with the aim to identify authentic histological CMV pneumonia [4]. Methods and major findings of our study During a 5-year period, autopsies were performed in patients who died while they presented a clinical picture of VAP with negative microbiological cultures (BAL, PSB, TA). In some patients who had an unexplained worsening of their respiratory status while under invasive mechanical ventilation, an OLB was performed. Immunocompromised patients were excluded from the study. ## Clinical presentation differences between immunocompromised and immunocompetent critically ill patients

The evidence suggests that CMV pneumonia behaves differently in immunocompromised versus immunocompetent critically ill patients, with the most striking difference being that immunocompromised patients are far more likely to develop life-threatening disease, whereas immunocompetent patients tend to have milder or less severe presentations.

### Typical symptoms and signs in immunocompromised patients
In immunocompromised patients, CMV pneumonia is described as one of the most often life-threatening forms of CMV disease [N3-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that life-threatening CMV pneumonia may develop in immunocompromised patients, with incidence varying by transplant type [N5-R3]. In ICU settings, active CMV infection is associated with worse outcomes for mechanically ventilated ICU patients [N3-F2]. This pattern is consistent with the broader literature that CMV reactivation is common in ICU patients and may worsen outcomes, especially in those with severe sepsis or high disease severity [N1-F1]. The clinical picture often includes respiratory failure, fever, and signs of severe pneumonia, with immunocompromised patients at higher risk of rapid clinical deterioration [N1-R5].

### Typical symptoms and signs in immunocompetent patients
In contrast, the evidence indicates that CMV pneumonia in immunocompetent hosts is often milder or even asymptomatic or self-limited [N3-R4]. Medscape notes that CMV infection in immunocompetent adults is mostly asymptomatic or mild [N5-R3]. The same source also says that severe CMV pneumonia in immunocompetent hosts is rare and may rarely require a full course of antiviral therapy [N1-R3]. The evidence from non-immunocompromised critically ill patients further suggests that CMV reactivation can occur in otherwise healthy ICU patients, but the clinical presentation may be non-specific and difficult to distinguish from other infections [N1-F1]. The non-immunocompromised ICU cohort also reports that CMV reactivation is common in ICU patients, but its role as a direct cause of mortality is debated [N1-F1].

### How severity and presentation differ by immune status
The evidence strongly supports a qualitative difference in disease severity: immunocompromised patients are much more likely to develop severe, life-threatening CMV pneumonia, while immunocompetent patients are more likely to have mild or even asymptomatic infection [N3-R4][N5-R3][N1-F1]. In ICU settings, active CMV infection is associated with worse outcomes for mechanically ventilated patients [N3-F2], and CMV reactivation is linked to increased ICU and hospital mortality, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and longer ICU stay [N1-F1]. For immunocompetent patients, the evidence suggests that CMV reactivation may still be clinically important, but the prognosis is generally better than in immunocompromised patients, with the prognosis of CMV pneumonia in immunocompetent hosts usually being good even in severe cases [N1-R3]. The distinction matters because it affects whether clinicians should treat or investigate more aggressively.

## Bottom line for presentation differences
Immunocompromised patients are more likely to present with severe, life-threatening CMV pneumonia and worse outcomes, while immunocompetent patients are more likely to present with mild, self-limited, or even asymptomatic CMV infection [N3-R4][N5-R3][N1-F1]. The evidence base is strongest for ICU patients, where CMV reactivation is common and may worsen outcomes, but the interpretation of that burden differs by immune status [N1-F1][N3-F2].

## Immune status differences and pathophysiology

The evidence points to a fundamental difference in how CMV pneumonia develops in immunocompromised versus immunocompetent hosts: immunocompromised hosts are at higher risk of CMV reactivation and more severe disease, while immunocompetent hosts may still develop CMV infection but with less severe or more benign outcomes.

### How immunocompromised hosts develop CMV pneumonia
In immunocompromised hosts, CMV pneumonia develops because the host’s immune defenses are weakened, allowing latent CMV to reactivate. The evidence describes CMV as a double-stranded DNA virus that remains latent in dendritic cells and monocytes after acute or primary infection [N1-F1]. In immunocompromised patients, CMV can reactivate during a state of decreased immunity or secondary infection with a new strain [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that CMV reactivation is common in ICU patients and may worsen outcomes, especially in patients with severe sepsis or high disease severity [N1-F1]. In the ICU-specific review, CMV is described as a pathogen that can directly injure organs such as the lung and that may also decrease host defenses against other microorganisms or enhance inflammatory responses [N3-F2]. For immunocompromised patients, this means that CMV pneumonia is not only a direct viral effect but also an immunopathological and possibly infectious complication [N3-F2].

### How immunocompetent hosts may develop CMV pneumonia
In immunocompetent hosts, CMV infection is usually asymptomatic or mild, and the evidence explicitly states that CMV infection in immunocompetent adults is mostly asymptomatic or mild and self-limited [N5-R3]. The same source also says that CMV pneumonia may be rare in immunocompetent hosts, with severe cases being rare and usually not requiring a full course of antiviral therapy [N1-R3]. The non-immunocompromised ICU evidence supports this by showing that CMV reactivation can occur in otherwise healthy ICU patients, but that the clinical presentation may be non-specific and difficult to distinguish from other infections [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that CMV seroprevalence is high in adults, but reactivation can still occur even in otherwise healthy individuals [N1-F1]. This suggests that immunocompetent hosts can develop CMV pneumonia, but it is much less common and less severe than in immunocompromised hosts.

### Biological mechanisms linking immune status to disease course
The evidence provides a clear mechanism linking immune status to disease course. In healthy individuals, cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes suppress viral gene replication [N1-F1]. When immunity is impaired, this suppression is inhibited, allowing latent CMV to enter the active lytic phase and cause disease [N1-F1]. This explains why immunocompromised hosts are more likely to develop severe CMV pneumonia. The evidence also suggests that CMV reactivation can affect disease course through multiple pathways: direct organ injury, immunopathological injury, and altered immune defenses that increase susceptibility to other infections [N3-F2]. For immunocompetent hosts, the same immune surveillance mechanisms are intact, which limits viral replication and typically keeps the infection mild [N1-F1].

## Bottom line for immune status and pathophysiology
Immunocompromised hosts develop CMV pneumonia because their immune defenses are weakened, allowing latent CMV to reactivate and cause severe lung disease [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Immunocompetent hosts may still develop CMV infection, but it is usually asymptomatic or mild and self-limited [N5-R3]. The biological mechanism is that cytotoxic T cells normally suppress CMV replication, but when immunity is impaired, viral replication is uncontrolled and disease becomes severe [N1-F1]. This explains the major difference in disease course between immune statuses [N1-F1][N3-F2].

## Diagnostic recognition and testing

The evidence supports a pragmatic diagnostic approach to CMV pneumonia in critically ill patients, with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and PCR being preferred tests, while chest imaging can raise suspicion in certain patterns. The interpretation of results is strongly affected by immune status: in immunocompromised patients, CMV is more likely to be clinically relevant and warrant treatment, whereas in immunocompetent patients, a positive result may reflect disease severity rather than direct pathogenicity [N2-R2][N4-R1][N1-F1][N3-F2].

### Preferred tests for diagnosing CMV pneumonia
The evidence clearly favors BAL combined with viral testing as the preferred approach. One source states that CMV PCR combined with a comprehensive clinical definition provides a pragmatic approach for the diagnosis of CMV pneumonitis [N2-R2]. Another study reports using CMV quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) in bronchial washing fluid [N2-R4], and a separate source notes that probable pneumonia is defined as detection of HCMV in BAL by viral isolation or DNA quantification combined with symptoms [N2-R5]. BAL is therefore central to the diagnostic algorithm. The evidence also supports bronchoscopy with BAL as a useful method to obtain samples, even though the exact technical details vary by source [N2-R3]. Overall, BAL with PCR-based testing is the preferred diagnostic strategy [N2-R2][N2-R4][N2-R5].

### When imaging findings should raise suspicion
Imaging findings can be very suggestive of CMV pneumonia. The radiology references describe diffuse ground-glass opacification, diffuse ground-glass nodules, secondary organizing pneumonia, and pleurisy as possible features [N4-R1]. Thin-section CT findings in immunocompromised patients with CMV pulmonary infection most commonly consist of a mixture of patterns, most commonly ground-glass attenuation [N4-R2]. Another case series shows CMV pneumonia presenting as pulmonary nodules on chest CT [N4-R3], and another source notes extensive patchy regions of ground-glass density within both lungs [N4-R5]. These findings are important because they may help clinicians suspect CMV pneumonia even before definitive testing, especially when the clinical picture is compatible with viral pneumonia. However, the evidence also emphasizes that CMV pneumonia can mimic other lung diseases, including lung cancer [N5-R5].

### How immune status affects interpretation of results
Immune status profoundly affects how results are interpreted. In immunocompromised patients, CMV reactivation is common and more likely to be clinically significant, with active CMV infection associated with worse outcomes for mechanically ventilated ICU patients [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence also suggests that CMV may be pathogenic in these patients, whereas in immunocompetent patients, the same findings may reflect disease severity rather than direct causation [N1-F1][N3-F2]. This means that a positive BAL result in an immunocompromised patient is more likely to indicate true disease requiring treatment, whereas in an immunocompetent patient, the same result may be better interpreted as a marker of severe illness rather than a direct cause of poor outcome [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that CMV reactivation can occur in non-immunocompromised ICU patients, but the clinical significance is debated [N1-F1].

## Bottom line for diagnostic recognition and testing
The preferred tests are bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and PCR-based testing [N2-R2][N2-R4][N2-R5]. Imaging findings such as diffuse ground-glass opacities, ground-glass nodules, and patchy ground-glass densities should raise suspicion of CMV pneumonia [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5]. Immune status strongly affects interpretation: in immunocompromised patients, a positive result is more likely to be clinically meaningful and require treatment, whereas in immunocompetent patients, a positive result may reflect disease severity rather than direct pathogenicity [N1-F1][N3-F2].

## ICU-specific recognition and red flags

The evidence indicates that ICU clinicians should watch for fever, respiratory failure, and other signs of deterioration, even when imaging appears normal. CMV pneumonia can be difficult to recognize early, especially in immunocompetent patients, and early recognition differs by immune status.

### Common ICU clues suggesting CMV pneumonia
The most common ICU clues are fever and respiratory failure. One source describes a case of CMV pneumonia requiring intensive care during the early stages of treatment for another disease, with the patient presenting with severe respiratory failure [N6-R1]. Another source notes that bronchoscopy with BAL was negative for Pneumocystis, but the diagnosis of CMV infection by serology involves detection of CMV markers [N2-R3]. This suggests that fever, respiratory failure, and the need for intensive care are central red flags. The broader ICU literature also emphasizes that CMV reactivation is common in ICU patients and may worsen outcomes [N1-F1], while another source specifically states that active CMV infection appears to be associated with worse outcomes for mechanically ventilated ICU patients [N3-F2].

### When to suspect CMV pneumonia despite normal imaging
The evidence supports that CMV pneumonia should be suspected despite normal chest imaging. The evidence notes that chest X-ray is frequently used to diagnose pneumonia, but the cited Facebook post is not itself diagnostic evidence; however, the broader context is that radiographic pneumonia can sometimes be missed initially [N6-R4]. More importantly, the ICU-specific review emphasizes that CMV reactivation can occur even in patients with normal imaging and that the diagnosis may not be obvious [N3-F2]. The evidence also indicates that CMV can mimic lung cancer and that CMV pneumonia may be missed on routine imaging [N5-R5]. Therefore, clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion when patients with ICU-acquired pneumonia-like illness do not improve with standard treatment, or when imaging is nondiagnostic.

### How early recognition differs between immune statuses
Early recognition differs substantially by immune status. In immunocompromised patients, CMV pneumonia is more likely to be severe and clinically urgent, so fever, respiratory failure, and ICU deterioration are especially strong red flags [N6-R1][N1-F1]. In contrast, in immunocompetent patients, CMV infection is often milder, asymptomatic, or self-limited, which means that early recognition may be more subtle and may rely on elevated suspicion in the context of ICU-acquired pneumonia or persistent fever [N3-R4][N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that CMV reactivation may be difficult to distinguish from other infections in non-immunocompromised ICU patients [N1-F1], so early recognition in immunocompetent patients may depend on clinical context rather than definitive imaging alone. In immunocompromised patients, however, the combination of fever, respiratory failure, and ICU deterioration is more compelling evidence for CMV pneumonia [N6-R1][N3-F2].

## Bottom line for ICU-specific recognition
Common ICU clues are fever and respiratory failure, especially when patients deteriorate after ICU admission or fail to improve with standard treatment [N6-R1][N2-R3]. CMV pneumonia should be suspected despite normal imaging because imaging can be nondiagnostic and CMV pneumonia can mimic other lung diseases [N5-R5]. Early recognition differs by immune status: immunocompromised patients are more likely to present with severe, urgent signs, whereas immunocompetent patients may present with milder or more subtle symptoms [N1-F1][N3-R4][N6-R1].

## Clinical presentation differences between immunocompromised and immunocompetent critically ill patients

The evidence suggests that CMV pneumonia behaves differently in immunocompromised versus immunocompetent critically ill patients, with the most striking difference being that immunocompromised patients are far more likely to develop life-threatening disease, whereas immunocompetent patients tend to have milder or less severe presentations.

### Typical symptoms and signs in immunocompromised patients
In immunocompromised patients, CMV pneumonia is described as one of the most often life-threatening forms of CMV disease [N3-R2]. The evidence also emphasizes that life-threatening CMV pneumonia may develop in immunocompromised patients, with incidence varying by transplant type [N5-R3]. In ICU settings, active CMV infection is associated with worse outcomes for mechanically ventilated ICU patients [N3-F2]. This pattern is consistent with the broader literature that CMV reactivation is common in ICU patients and may worsen outcomes, especially in those with severe sepsis or high disease severity [N1-F1]. The clinical picture often includes respiratory failure, fever, and signs of severe pneumonia, with immunocompromised patients at higher risk of rapid clinical deterioration [N1-R5].

### Typical symptoms and signs in immunocompetent patients
In contrast, the evidence indicates that CMV pneumonia in immunocompetent hosts is often milder or even asymptomatic or self-limited [N3-R4]. Medscape notes that CMV infection in immunocompetent adults is mostly asymptomatic or mild [N5-R3]. The same source also says that severe CMV pneumonia in immunocompetent hosts is rare and may rarely require a full course of antiviral therapy [N1-R3]. The evidence from non-immunocompromised critically ill patients further suggests that CMV reactivation can occur in otherwise healthy ICU patients, but the clinical presentation may be non-specific and difficult to distinguish from other infections [N1-F1]. The non-immunocompromised ICU cohort also reports that CMV reactivation is common in ICU patients, but its role as a direct cause of mortality is debated [N1-F1].

### How severity and presentation differ by immune status
The evidence strongly supports a qualitative difference in disease severity: immunocompromised patients are much more likely to develop severe, life-threatening CMV pneumonia, while immunocompetent patients are more likely to have mild or even asymptomatic infection [N3-R4][N5-R3][N1-F1]. In ICU settings, active CMV infection is associated with worse outcomes for mechanically ventilated patients [N3-F2], and CMV reactivation is linked to increased ICU and hospital mortality, prolonged mechanical ventilation, and longer ICU stay [N1-F1]. For immunocompetent patients, the evidence suggests that CMV reactivation may still be clinically important, but the prognosis is generally better than in immunocompromised patients, with the prognosis of CMV pneumonia in immunocompetent hosts usually being good even in severe cases [N1-R3]. The distinction matters because it affects whether clinicians should treat or investigate more aggressively.

## Bottom line for presentation differences
Immunocompromised patients are more likely to present with severe, life-threatening CMV pneumonia and worse outcomes, while immunocompetent patients are more likely to present with mild, self-limited, or even asymptomatic CMV infection [N3-R4][N5-R3][N1-F1]. The evidence base is strongest for ICU patients, where CMV reactivation is common and may worsen outcomes, but the interpretation of that burden differs by immune status [N1-F1][N3-F2].

## Immune status differences and pathophysiology

The evidence points to a fundamental difference in how CMV pneumonia develops in immunocompromised versus immunocompetent hosts: immunocompromised hosts are at higher risk of CMV reactivation and more severe disease, while immunocompetent hosts may still develop CMV infection but with less severe or more benign outcomes.

### How immunocompromised hosts develop CMV pneumonia
In immunocompromised hosts, CMV pneumonia develops because the host’s immune defenses are weakened, allowing latent CMV to reactivate. The evidence describes CMV as a double-stranded DNA virus that remains latent in dendritic cells and monocytes after acute or primary infection [N1-F1]. In immunocompromised patients, CMV can reactivate during a state of decreased immunity or secondary infection with a new strain [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that CMV reactivation is common in ICU patients and may worsen outcomes, especially in patients with severe sepsis or high disease severity [N1-F1]. In the ICU-specific review, CMV is described as a pathogen that can directly injure organs such as the lung and that may also decrease host defenses against other microorganisms or enhance inflammatory responses [N3-F2]. For immunocompromised patients, this means that CMV pneumonia is not only a direct viral effect but also an immunopathological and possibly infectious complication [N3-F2].

### How immunocompetent hosts may develop CMV pneumonia
In immunocompetent hosts, CMV infection is usually asymptomatic or mild, and the evidence explicitly states that CMV infection in immunocompetent adults is mostly asymptomatic or mild and self-limited [N5-R3]. The same source also says that CMV pneumonia may be rare in immunocompetent hosts, with severe cases being rare and usually not requiring a full course of antiviral therapy [N1-R3]. The non-immunocompromised ICU evidence supports this by showing that CMV reactivation can occur in otherwise healthy ICU patients, but that the clinical presentation may be non-specific and difficult to distinguish from other infections [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that CMV seroprevalence is high in adults, but reactivation can still occur even in otherwise healthy individuals [N1-F1]. This suggests that immunocompetent hosts can develop CMV pneumonia, but it is much less common and less severe than in immunocompromised hosts.

### Biological mechanisms linking immune status to disease course
The evidence provides a clear mechanism linking immune status to disease course. In healthy individuals, cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes suppress viral gene replication [N1-F1]. When immunity is impaired, this suppression is inhibited, allowing latent CMV to enter the active lytic phase and cause disease [N1-F1]. This explains why immunocompromised hosts are more likely to develop severe CMV pneumonia. The evidence also suggests that CMV reactivation can affect disease course through multiple pathways: direct organ injury, immunopathological injury, and altered immune defenses that increase susceptibility to other infections [N3-F2]. For immunocompetent hosts, the same immune surveillance mechanisms are intact, which limits viral replication and typically keeps the infection mild [N1-F1].

## Bottom line for immune status and pathophysiology
Immunocompromised hosts develop CMV pneumonia because their immune defenses are weakened, allowing latent CMV to reactivate and cause severe lung disease [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Immunocompetent hosts may still develop CMV infection, but it is usually asymptomatic or mild and self-limited [N5-R3]. The biological mechanism is that cytotoxic T cells normally suppress CMV replication, but when immunity is impaired, viral replication is uncontrolled and disease becomes severe [N1-F1]. This explains the major difference in disease course between immune statuses [N1-F1][N3-F2].

## Diagnostic recognition and testing

The evidence supports a pragmatic diagnostic approach to CMV pneumonia in critically ill patients, with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and PCR being preferred tests, while chest imaging can raise suspicion in certain patterns. The interpretation of results is strongly affected by immune status: in immunocompromised patients, CMV is more likely to be clinically relevant and warrant treatment, whereas in immunocompetent patients, a positive result may reflect disease severity rather than direct pathogenicity [N2-R2][N4-R1][N1-F1][N3-F2].

### Preferred tests for diagnosing CMV pneumonia
The evidence clearly favors BAL combined with viral testing as the preferred approach. One source states that CMV PCR combined with a comprehensive clinical definition provides a pragmatic approach for the diagnosis of CMV pneumonitis [N2-R2]. Another study reports using CMV quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) in bronchial washing fluid [N2-R4], and a separate source notes that probable pneumonia is defined as detection of HCMV in BAL by viral isolation or DNA quantification combined with symptoms [N2-R5]. BAL is therefore central to the diagnostic algorithm. The evidence also supports bronchoscopy with BAL as a useful method to obtain samples, even though the exact technical details vary by source [N2-R3]. Overall, BAL with PCR-based testing is the preferred diagnostic strategy [N2-R2][N2-R4][N2-R5].

### When imaging findings should raise suspicion
Imaging findings can be very suggestive of CMV pneumonia. The radiology references describe diffuse ground-glass opacification, diffuse ground-glass nodules, secondary organizing pneumonia, and pleurisy as possible features [N4-R1]. Thin-section CT findings in immunocompromised patients with CMV pulmonary infection most commonly consist of a mixture of patterns, most commonly ground-glass attenuation [N4-R2]. Another case series shows CMV pneumonia presenting as pulmonary nodules on chest CT [N4-R3], and another source notes extensive patchy regions of ground-glass density within both lungs [N4-R5]. These findings are important because they may help clinicians suspect CMV pneumonia even before definitive testing, especially when the clinical picture is compatible with viral pneumonia. However, the evidence also emphasizes that CMV pneumonia can mimic other lung diseases, including lung cancer [N5-R5].

### How immune status affects interpretation of results
Immune status profoundly affects how results are interpreted. In immunocompromised patients, CMV reactivation is common and more likely to be clinically significant, with active CMV infection associated with worse outcomes for mechanically ventilated ICU patients [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence also suggests that CMV may be pathogenic in these patients, whereas in immunocompetent patients, the same findings may reflect disease severity rather than direct causation [N1-F1][N3-F2]. This means that a positive BAL result in an immunocompromised patient is more likely to indicate true disease requiring treatment, whereas in an immunocompetent patient, the same result may be better interpreted as a marker of severe illness rather than a direct cause of poor outcome [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that CMV reactivation can occur in non-immunocompromised ICU patients, but the clinical significance is debated [N1-F1].

## Bottom line for diagnostic recognition and testing
The preferred tests are bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and PCR-based testing [N2-R2][N2-R4][N2-R5]. Imaging findings such as diffuse ground-glass opacities, ground-glass nodules, and patchy ground-glass densities should raise suspicion of CMV pneumonia [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5]. Immune status strongly affects interpretation: in immunocompromised patients, a positive result is more likely to be clinically meaningful and require treatment, whereas in immunocompetent patients, a positive result may reflect disease severity rather than direct pathogenicity [N1-F1][N3-F2].

## ICU-specific recognition and red flags

The evidence indicates that ICU clinicians should watch for fever, respiratory failure, and other signs of deterioration, even when imaging appears normal. CMV pneumonia can be difficult to recognize early, especially in immunocompetent patients, and early recognition differs by immune status.

### Common ICU clues suggesting CMV pneumonia
The most common ICU clues are fever and respiratory failure. One source describes a case of CMV pneumonia requiring intensive care during the early stages of treatment for another disease, with the patient presenting with severe respiratory failure [N6-R1]. Another source notes that bronchoscopy with BAL was negative for Pneumocystis, but the diagnosis of CMV infection by serology involves detection of CMV markers [N2-R3]. This suggests that fever, respiratory failure, and the need for intensive care are central red flags. The broader ICU literature also emphasizes that CMV reactivation is common in ICU patients and may worsen outcomes [N1-F1], while another source specifically states that active CMV infection appears to be associated with worse outcomes for mechanically ventilated ICU patients [N3-F2].

### When to suspect CMV pneumonia despite normal imaging
The evidence supports that CMV pneumonia should be suspected despite normal chest imaging. The evidence notes that chest X-ray is frequently used to diagnose pneumonia, but the cited Facebook post is not itself diagnostic evidence; however, the broader context is that radiographic pneumonia can sometimes be missed initially [N6-R4]. More importantly, the ICU-specific review emphasizes that CMV reactivation can occur even in patients with normal imaging and that the diagnosis may not be obvious [N3-F2]. The evidence also indicates that CMV can mimic lung cancer and that CMV pneumonia may be missed on routine imaging [N5-R5]. Therefore, clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion when patients with ICU-acquired pneumonia-like illness do not improve with standard treatment, or when imaging is nondiagnostic.

Early recognition differs substantially by immune status. The evidence also suggests that CMV reactivation may be difficult to distinguish from other infections in non-immunocompromised ICU patients [N1-F1], so early recognition in immunocompetent patients may depend on clinical context rather than definitive imaging alone. In immunocompromised patients, however, the combination of fever, respiratory failure, and ICU deterioration is more compelling evidence for CMV pneumonia [N6-R1][N3-F2].

## Bottom line for ICU-specific recognition
Common ICU clues are fever and respiratory failure, especially when patients deteriorate after ICU admission or fail to improve with standard treatment [N6-R1][N2-R3]. CMV pneumonia should be suspected despite normal imaging because imaging can be nondiagnostic and CMV pneumonia can mimic other lung diseases [N5-R5]. Early recognition differs by immune status: immunocompromised patients are more likely to present with severe, urgent signs, whereas immunocompetent patients may present with milder or more subtle symptoms [N1-F1][N3-R4][N6-R1].

The main distinction is qualitative: immunocompromised patients are more likely to develop severe, life-threatening lung involvement and worse outcomes, whereas immunocompetent patients are more likely to have mild, self-limited, or even asymptomatic infection [N3-R4][N5-R3][N1-F1]. This difference is not only clinical but also biological: in immunocompromised hosts, CMV reactivation is more likely to lead to severe disease, while in immunocompetent hosts, the same reactivation is often less severe and may be better interpreted as a marker of disease severity rather than direct pathogenicity [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The final answer is therefore best organized around presentation, recognition, immune pathophysiology, and ICU-specific red flags.

---

## 1) Clinical presentation differs by immune status

### Immunocompromised patients
Immunocompromised patients are at much higher risk of severe and life-threatening CMV pneumonia. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that CMV pneumonia is one of the most often life-threatening forms of CMV disease, especially in immunocompromised patients [N3-R2]. In ICU settings, active CMV infection is associated with worse outcomes for mechanically ventilated ICU patients [N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that CMV reactivation is common in ICU patients and may worsen outcomes, especially in patients with severe sepsis or high disease severity [N1-F1]. In this group, the clinical presentation is typically more severe: fever, respiratory failure, and signs of acute lung injury are common, and the disease course is often more aggressive [N1-R5][N3-F2].

### Immunocompetent patients
In contrast, CMV pneumonia in immunocompetent hosts is much less severe. The evidence states that CMV infection in immunocompetent adults is mostly asymptomatic or mild and self-limited [N5-R3]. The same source adds that severe CMV pneumonia may be rare in immunocompetent hosts, and that severe cases may rarely require a full course of antiviral therapy [N1-R3]. The evidence from non-immunocompromised critically ill patients reinforces this: CMV reactivation can occur in otherwise healthy ICU patients, but the clinical presentation may be non-specific and difficult to distinguish from other infections [N1-F1]. So, in immunocompetent patients, the clinical picture is often milder, and the presence of CMV infection may not translate into the same level of urgent respiratory or systemic compromise.

### How severity and presentation differ by immune status
The core difference is severity. Immunocompromised patients are more likely to present with severe respiratory failure, ICU deterioration, and a worse prognosis [N6-R1][N1-F1][N3-F2]. Immunocompetent patients are more likely to present with mild, self-limited, or even asymptomatic infection [N5-R3][N3-R4]. The evidence also notes that CMV reactivation may be common in ICU patients, but whether it is a true cause of clinical deterioration or merely a marker of disease severity is still debated [N1-F1]. This matters because it changes how clinicians interpret clinical deterioration: in immunocompromised patients, a worsening course is more likely to be pathogenic; in immunocompetent patients, it may reflect other causes or simply severe illness.

## 2) Diagnostic recognition and testing

The evidence supports a pragmatic diagnostic approach centered on bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and PCR-based testing. One source explicitly says that CMV PCR combined with a comprehensive clinical definition provides a pragmatic approach for the diagnosis of CMV pneumonitis [N2-R2]. Another source reports using CMV quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) in bronchial washing fluid [N2-R4], and another defines probable pneumonia as detection of HCMV in BAL by viral isolation or DNA quantification combined with symptoms [N2-R5]. BAL is therefore the preferred method for obtaining diagnostic material, while PCR is the preferred molecular test.

### Preferred tests
The preferred tests are:
- bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage [N2-R3]
- CMV PCR, qRT-PCR, or similar viral load testing [N2-R2][N2-R4][N2-R5]

### When imaging findings should raise suspicion
Imaging can be highly suggestive of CMV pneumonia. The radiology references describe diffuse ground-glass opacification, diffuse ground-glass nodules, secondary organizing pneumonia, and pleurisy as possible features [N4-R1]. Thin-section CT findings in immunocompromised patients most commonly consist of a mixture of patterns, most commonly ground-glass attenuation [N4-R2]. Other sources note CMV pneumonia presenting as pulmonary nodules on chest CT and extensive patchy regions of ground-glass density within both lungs [N4-R3][N4-R5]. These imaging patterns should raise suspicion, especially when they occur in a patient with fever, respiratory failure, or other signs of pneumonia.

### How immune status affects interpretation of results
Immune status profoundly affects how results are interpreted. In immunocompromised patients, CMV reactivation is common and more likely to be clinically significant, with active CMV infection associated with worse outcomes in mechanically ventilated ICU patients [N1-F1][N3-F2]. In these patients, a positive BAL result is more likely to indicate true disease requiring treatment. In contrast, in immunocompetent patients, the same findings may reflect disease severity rather than direct pathogenicity [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence also notes that CMV can mimic lung cancer and that CMV pneumonia may be difficult to distinguish from other lung diseases [N5-R5]. This means that clinicians should be cautious about treating immunocompetent patients with CMV-positive BAL results unless the clinical context strongly supports active disease.

## 3) Immune status differences and pathophysiology

The evidence explains the difference in disease course as a matter of immune control. In healthy individuals, cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes suppress viral gene replication [N1-F1]. When immunity is impaired, this suppression is inhibited, allowing latent CMV to enter the active lytic phase and cause disease [N1-F1]. This is why immunocompromised hosts are more likely to develop severe CMV pneumonia [N1-F1][N3-F2].

### How immunocompromised hosts develop CMV pneumonia
Immunocompromised hosts develop CMV pneumonia because their immune defenses are weakened, allowing latent CMV to reactivate. The evidence describes CMV as a double-stranded DNA virus that remains latent in dendritic cells and monocytes after acute or primary infection [N1-F1]. In immunocompromised patients, reactivation can occur during a state of decreased immunity or secondary infection with a new strain [N1-F1]. The ICU-specific review adds that CMV can directly injure organs such as the lung and may also decrease host defenses against other microorganisms or enhance inflammatory responses [N3-F2]. So, CMV pneumonia in immunocompromised patients is not only a direct viral effect but also an immunopathological and possibly infectious complication.

### How immunocompetent hosts may develop CMV pneumonia
Immunocompetent hosts may still develop CMV infection, but it is usually asymptomatic or mild. The evidence explicitly states that CMV infection in immunocompetent adults is mostly asymptomatic or mild and self-limited [N5-R3]. The same source also says that severe CMV pneumonia may be rare in immunocompetent hosts, and that severe cases may rarely require a full course of antiviral therapy [N1-R3]. The non-immunocompromised ICU evidence supports this by showing that CMV reactivation can occur in otherwise healthy ICU patients, but that the clinical presentation may be non-specific and difficult to distinguish from other infections [N1-F1]. This suggests that immunocompetent hosts can develop CMV pneumonia, but the disease is much less severe and less likely to be life-threatening.

### Biological mechanisms linking immune status to disease course
The biological mechanism is straightforward: cytotoxic T cells normally suppress CMV replication, but when immunity is impaired, viral replication is uncontrolled and disease becomes severe [N1-F1]. This explains why immunocompromised hosts are more likely to develop severe CMV pneumonia, while immunocompetent hosts are more likely to have mild or asymptomatic infection [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence also suggests that CMV reactivation can affect disease course through multiple pathways: direct organ injury, immunopathological injury, and altered immune defenses that increase susceptibility to other infections [N3-F2].

## 4) ICU-specific recognition and red flags

In the ICU, the red flags for CMV pneumonia are fever and respiratory failure, especially when patients deteriorate after ICU admission or fail to improve with standard treatment. One source describes a case of CMV pneumonia requiring intensive care during the early stages of treatment for another disease, with the patient presenting with severe respiratory failure [N6-R1]. Another source notes that bronchoscopy with BAL was negative for Pneumocystis, but the diagnosis of CMV infection by serology involves detection of CMV markers [N2-R3]. This suggests that fever, respiratory failure, and ICU deterioration are central red flags.

### Common ICU clues suggesting CMV pneumonia
The common ICU clues are:
- fever
- respiratory failure
- ICU deterioration or need for intensive care [N6-R1][N2-R3]

### When to suspect CMV pneumonia despite normal imaging
CMV pneumonia should be suspected despite normal imaging because imaging can be nondiagnostic and CMV pneumonia can mimic other lung diseases [N5-R5]. The evidence also indicates that CMV reactivation can occur even in patients with normal imaging and that the diagnosis may not be obvious [N3-F2]. This means that clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion when patients with ICU-acquired pneumonia-like illness do not improve with standard treatment, or when imaging is nondiagnostic.

### How early recognition differs between immune statuses
Early recognition differs by immune status. In immunocompromised patients, CMV pneumonia is more likely to be severe and clinically urgent, so fever, respiratory failure, and ICU deterioration are especially strong red flags [N6-R1][N1-F1]. In contrast, in immunocompetent patients, CMV infection is often milder, asymptomatic, or self-limited, which means that early recognition may be more subtle and may rely on elevated suspicion in the context of ICU-acquired pneumonia or persistent fever [N3-R4][N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that CMV reactivation may be difficult to distinguish from other infections in non-immunocompromised ICU patients [N1-F1], so early recognition in immunocompetent patients may depend on clinical context rather than definitive imaging alone.

---

## Bottom line

The presentation and recognition of lung involvement in CMV pneumonia differ fundamentally by immune status:

- **Immunocompromised patients** are more likely to present with severe, life-threatening disease, including fever, respiratory failure, and ICU deterioration, and more likely to require treatment because CMV reactivation is clinically significant [N3-R2][N1-F1][N3-F2][N6-R1].
- **Immunocompetent patients** are more likely to present with mild, self-limited, or even asymptomatic infection, and a positive CMV result may better be interpreted as a marker of disease severity rather than direct causation [N5-R3][N1-R3][N1-F1].
- **Diagnostic recognition** favors bronchoscopy with BAL and PCR-based testing, with imaging patterns such as diffuse ground-glass opacities, ground-glass nodules, and patchy ground-glass densities raising suspicion [N2-R2][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].
- **ICU recognition** is especially challenging because fever and respiratory failure are common red flags, but CMV pneumonia can occur despite normal imaging and may mimic other lung diseases [N6-R1][N2-R3][N5-R5][N3-F2].
- **Immune status affects interpretation**: in immunocompromised patients, a positive result is more likely to be meaningful; in immunocompetent patients, the same result may reflect severity rather than pathogenicity [N1-F1][N3-F2].

Overall, the distinction is not just one of severity, but one of biological plausibility, clinical urgency, and treatment decision-making [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-R3].
